title: channel-merging-lazy-kv-handoff-notes
summary: Exploratory notes for a unified channel model that merges prefill and decode lanes via lazy KV handoff; aims to improve tail latency, preserve batching efficiency, and simplify kernel scheduling without brittle early handoffs.
content:
Purpose:
This doc sketches an alternative to the conventional strict prefill->decode handoff. Instead of an immediate, synchronous transfer of attention/KV ownership at prefill end, we propose a channel-merging model with lazy KV handoff: prefill work can be merged into an active decode channel on demand, with a small rendezvous handshake that triggers KV residency transfer only when decode emission actually needs it.

Why? (motivation)
- Observed inefficiency: tight, eager handoffs create short-lived KV residency and thrash when streams are cancelled or prefill windows are trimmed.
- Microbatch mismatch: prefill batches and decode tokens often produce different kernel footprints; copying/locking KV eagerly increases contention (GPU memory + memcpy) and harms throughput for cold tail events.
- Priority inversion: higher-priority interactive streams sometimes wait on earlier prefill handshakes for lower value background prefetches.

Goals (measurable):
- Maintain or reduce p99 tail for interactive decode streams (target: -5–10% p99 improvement vs current eager-handoff baseline).
- Preserve effective batch sizes for throughput-critical workloads (<= 5% throughput regression in 90% workloads).
- Reduce unnecessary KV transfers/memcpy events (target: 15–30% fewer handoff copy ops in mixed workloads).
- Simplify kernel affinity rules and reduce scheduling staleness.

Core idea (high level):
1) Channel abstraction: treat "prefill" and "decode" as logical channels that can be merged at runtime. Each client stream has a small channel descriptor (state machine) that records: sequence ranges owned by prefill, sequence ranges emitted by decode, and a rendezvous token for the KV block.

2) Lazy KV handoff: instead of moving KV immediately at prefill completion, prefill tags the KV entry as "mergeable". When a decode emit request needs access to KV for a given prefix/slot, the scheduler triggers a short, prioritized handshake to elevate the mergeable KV into residency for the target decode slot. If decode never requests it (cancellation, short responses), no costly transfer occurs.

3) Merge windows: define a small sliding window (configurable, default 2–8 tokens) where prefill and decode can co-reside logically and be scheduled together to exploit contiguous kernel runs. Outside the window, normal isolation applies. The window bounds give a controlled state where lazy handoff is allowed without broad staleness risk.

Key mechanisms and heuristics:
- Rendezvous token: a tiny metadata object (64–128 bytes) that points to KV shards + epoch/version + preferred kernel affinity. Tokens are cheap to move and are used to request KV residency rather than copying full caches.
- On-demand elevation: when decode needs KV for token t, scheduler checks: is token t present as mergeable? If yes, escalate with high priority microbatch (attempt local kernel that supports co-resident prefill work). If not, fallback to current eager path (fetch from persistent cache).
- Priority buckets: streams are classified into buckets (interactive-high, interactive-low, background). Elevation requests from higher buckets preempt lower bucket copy operations.
- Kernel affinity tags: rendezvous token includes preferred kernel/launch parameters (e.g., preferred kernel optimized for long sequences, quantized path). Scheduler tries to match contiguous tokens with same affinity into a single kernel launch to reduce kernel churn.
- Backpressure semantics: marking KV as mergeable keeps it eligible for compaction after a TTL (short, e.g., 50–200 ms). If the system is under memory pressure, mergeable entries are the first to be demoted.

Microbatch composition rules (sketch):
- Window-based grouping: when building a microbatch, prioritize grouping tokens that are within the same merge window and share kernel affinity.
- Fill-first for latency: for interactive-high streams, include pending decode emissions even if it reduces ideal batch depth; rely on kernel affinity to keep cost reasonable. For background/throughput lanes, prefer deeper batches with lower priority handoff.

KV staleness & correctness:
- Versioning: rendezvous tokens carry version ids for KV snapshots. During elevation, scheduler verifies token.version == current.version. If mismatch (background eviction or model change), trigger a quick fetch/regen like existing fetch path.
- Deterministic fallback: decode must be able to continue without merge if elevation fails; the fallback path must have bounded extra latency and preserve response correctness.

Failure modes and mitigation:
- Preemption storms: many elevation requests simultaneously could stress memcpy pathways. Mitigation: rate limiter per-device and per-tenant, prioritized queues, and coalescing of requests for same shards.
- Excessive churn: mergeable tags might keep many KV slices alive if TTLs are misconfigured. Mitigation: adaptive TTL based on device memory pressure and recent elevation hit rate.
- Priority inversion from long-running prefill: enforce a max-merge-span and ability to forcibly demote mergeable entries for higher-priority interactive needs.

Observability and instrumentation:
- Metrics to emit: elevation_request_count, elevation_success_rate, elevation_latency_distribution (p50/p90/p99), mergeable_eviction_rate, memcpy_bytes_saved_estimate, kernel_churn_rate, microbatch_composition_size_by_bucket.
- Tracing: attach rendezvous token id in RPC traces so we can correlate a decode emission with the prefill origin and inspect whether lazy handoff triggered; helpful to debug incorrect demotions.

Experiment plan (A/B):
- A: baseline (current eager handoff) on canary cluster.
- B: channel-merging with lazy handoff, conservative TTL (50ms), merge-window=3, rate limit 100 elev/sec/device.
- Run mixed traffic replay (interactive-heavy + background embedding prefetch) across both. Measure p99/p50 latencies, throughput, memcpy op counts, and elevation hit/miss rates.
- Success criteria: p99 interactive reduces or stays equal, throughput down <=5%, memcpy ops reduced >=15%.

Prototype implementation notes (engineering constraints):
- Rendezvous token must be serializable in our current RPC frame and cheap to attach to existing stream state.
- The scheduler path for elevation must be in fast path (avoid extra RPC round trips). Likely implement as a priority micro-op scheduled on device worker thread that upgrades the residency pointer.
- Kernel drivers: slight change to kernels to accept a token->kv lookup path so they can run if KV resident or trigger local fetch fallback if not.

Open questions / unresolved tradeoffs:
- TTL sizing: short TTL reduces memory pressure but may cause too many misses; long TTL consumes memory. Need workload-based adaptive TTL heuristic.
- Merge-window sizing vs kernel efficiencies: small windows reduce incorrect merges but may miss batching opportunities.
- Is rendezvous token enough to avoid stale KV correctness issues in multi-version rollout scenarios? Might require stronger snapshot guarantees.

Action items / next steps:
- Implement token schema and wire it through stream state (owner: Marcus). Timeline: 2 weeks for baseline proto.
- Add elevation micro-op to scheduler and priority queue hooks (owner: Ravi). Timeline: 2–3 weeks.
- Create mixed-workload replay harness to measure memcpy ops and p99 tail (owner: Lina). Timeline: 1 week.
- Run internal canary, collect metrics, iterate on TTL and merge-window sizing.

Notes to self / brainstorming fragments:
- Could combine with existing prefix caching heuristics: prefill that was fully predicted by prefix cache = immediate demote (no merge).
- Think about a "soft-lock" for mergeable entries rather than an exclusive lock to avoid blocking background compaction.
- Consider exposing per-tenant knobs for conservative vs aggressive merge policies.

References and comparisons:
- Current eager handoff: immediate ownership transfer at prefill end, straightforward but leads to many short-lived resids.
- Other ideas: pre-compute compacted_kv snapshots for tiny decodes (costly to compute for long contexts).

Bottom line: channel-merging with lazy KV handoff looks promising for mixed traffic where many prefill windows don't result in long decodes and where priority isolation matters. The key is implementing a cheap rendezvous token + prioritized elevation path and careful TTL/rate-limit heuristics. Prototype and measurements will determine whether kernel affinity gains outweigh added scheduler complexity.
